purpose: This medication is used to treat certain types of advanced colorectal cancer (colon or rectal cancer) or stomach cancer that has spread to other parts of the body. It is typically used when other cancer treatments have already been tried and have stopped working. Your doctor chose this medicine to help slow the growth of cancer cells.
how_it_works: This medicine is actually two drugs working together as a team. Trifluridine is the cancer-fighting part — it gets into cancer cells and messes up their DNA so they cannot grow and multiply. Tipiracil is the helper — it keeps your body from breaking down the trifluridine too quickly, so it can stay active in your body long enough to do its job.
common_side_effects: The most common side effects include low blood cell counts (which can make you feel tired, increase your risk of infection, or cause easy bruising or bleeding), nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, loss of appetite, and fatigue or weakness. Many patients also experience low white blood cell counts, so your doctor will monitor your blood regularly.
warnings: This medicine can seriously lower your white blood cells, red blood cells, and platelets — so watch for signs of infection like fever or chills, unusual bleeding, or extreme tiredness and call your doctor right away. Do not take this medicine if you are pregnant, as it can harm an unborn baby — use reliable birth control during treatment and for a period after. Tell your doctor about all other medications you are taking. Never share this medicine with anyone else.
typical_dosing: The usual dose is taken by mouth twice a day — once in the morning and once in the evening — with food. It is taken for the first 5 days of each week for 2 weeks in a row, followed by a 2-week break. This 4-week cycle is then repeated. Your doctor will calculate your exact dose based on your body size and will adjust it if needed based on how your body responds.
